name: HTMX UI
description: Tailwind CSS components for htmx apps. Plain HTML, themeable with CSS variables, dark mode built in.

pages.title: Introduction
pages.description: HTMX UI is a set of Tailwind CSS components for apps where the server renders HTML and htmx swaps it into the page.

sections.text: Installation Add the package to a new or existing Bun project. Theming Override design tokens or build a custom theme. Dark mode How dark mode works and how to add a switcher. Components Browse every component with live examples.

sections.title: What it is
sections.text: Most component libraries assume a JavaScript framework owns the page. HTMX UI assumes the opposite: your server returns HTML, htmx swaps it in, and components need to look right and keep working when they arrive inside a fragment. So every component is: Markup and classes. A button is <button class="btn btn-primary">. Any server language can render it. Styled with Tailwind v4. Component classes live in @layer components, so a utility class on the same element always wins. Themed with CSS variables. Colours and radius are variables like --primary and --radius, exposed to Tailwind as bg-primary, text-muted-foreground and so on. Behaviour only where needed. Things like copy buttons and the mobile sidebar are tiny TypeScript modules that re-run after every htmx swap.

sections.title: Working with htmx
sections.text: The entry script calls initComponents(document) once the page loads, and again with each newly inserted element on the htmx:after:process event. Each initialiser only touches elements it hasn't seen yet (it marks them with data-init), so a fragment's components come alive without anything running twice. app.ts import "htmx.org"; import { initComponents } from "htmx-ui"; document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => initComponents(document)); document.addEventListener("htmx:after:process", (e) => initComponents(e.target ?? document)); Why not htmx:after:swap? In htmx 4, htmx:after:swap is dispatched on the element that made the request, so its target is not the new content. htmx:after:process fires on each element htmx inserts, which is exactly what needs initialising.

sections.title: What it's built on
sections.text: htmx 4 for requests and swaps. Tailwind CSS v4 for styling and tokens. Bun for bundling, the dev server and tests. Nunjucks macros (optional) for less repetitive markup.

pages.title: Installation
pages.description: Start a new HTMX UI site with one command, or add the components to an app that already uses Tailwind CSS v4 and htmx.

sections.text: Commands are shown for bun, npm, pnpm and yarn. Pick yours once; every command block on the site remembers the choice.

sections.title: Packages
sections.text: Package What it is htmx-ui The components: CSS classes, design tokens, dark mode and small behaviours. Works with any bundler. htmx-ui-engine Builds a site from Nunjucks pages: htmx-ui dev, build and preview, on Bun or Node. See Engine. create-htmx-ui Scaffolds a new site that uses both.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.text: Dependency Version Why Tailwind CSS 4.x Component styles use @apply and @theme. htmx 4.x Fragment swaps; components initialise inside new content. Bun or Node Bun 1.2.3+ / Node 22.12+ For the engine. With your own bundler, any that handles TypeScript and CSS imports works.

sections.title: New project
sections.text: Create a site, install it and start the dev server: bun create htmx-ui my-site cd my-site bun install bun run dev npm create htmx-ui my-site cd my-site npm install npm run dev pnpm create htmx-ui my-site cd my-site pnpm install pnpm run dev yarn create htmx-ui my-site cd my-site yarn install yarn run dev You get pages/ (one file per route), a layout with a theme toggle, Tailwind with the library's styles, an htmx button talking to a mock endpoint, and dev, build and preview scripts. A site created with bun runs on Bun; with npm, pnpm or yarn it runs on Node, with Vite. Open http://localhost:3000 and edit pages/index.html.

sections.title: Add the engine to a project
1. Install
sections.text: bun add htmx-ui htmx.org bun add -d htmx-ui-engine tailwindcss npm install htmx-ui htmx.org npm install -D htmx-ui-engine tailwindcss pnpm add htmx-ui htmx.org pnpm add -D htmx-ui-engine tailwindcss yarn add htmx-ui htmx.org yarn add -D htmx-ui-engine tailwindcss Then the Tailwind integration for the runtime you'll build with. On Bun: Terminal bun add -d bun-plugin-tailwind On Node (npm, pnpm or yarn), Vite and its Tailwind plugin: bun add -d vite @tailwindcss/vite npm install -D vite @tailwindcss/vite pnpm add -D vite @tailwindcss/vite yarn add -D vite @tailwindcss/vite

sections.title: 2. Add the scripts
sections.text: package.json { "scripts": { "dev": "htmx-ui dev", "build": "htmx-ui build", "preview": "htmx-ui preview" } }

sections.title: 3. Import the styles
sections.text: Import Tailwind first, then the library. The @source line tells Tailwind where your own markup lives. styles.css @import "tailwindcss"; @import "htmx-ui/styles.css"; @source "./";

sections.title: 4. Initialise components
sections.text: app.ts import "htmx.org"; import "./styles.css"; import { initComponents } from "htmx-ui"; import { initTheme } from "htmx-ui/theme"; document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { initTheme(); initComponents(document); }); // htmx 4 fires htmx:after:process on each newly inserted element document.addEventListener("htmx:after:process", (e) => { initComponents((e.target as ParentNode) ?? document); });

sections.title: 5. Add a layout and a page
sections.text: asset() makes the script path relative to whichever page is rendering, so the bundler finds it from any depth. layouts/base.html <!doctype html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta charset="utf-8" /> <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" /> <title>{% block title %}My site{% endblock %}</title> <script type="module" src="{{ asset('app.ts') }}"></script> </head> <body class="bg-background text-foreground"> {% block content %}{% endblock %} </body> </html> pages/index.html {% extends "layouts/base.html" %} {% block content %}<button class="btn btn-primary">It works</button>{% endblock %} bun run dev npm run dev pnpm run dev yarn run dev

sections.title: Existing project
sections.text: If the app already has Tailwind v4, htmx and a bundler, it only needs the components: bun add htmx-ui npm install htmx-ui pnpm add htmx-ui yarn add htmx-ui Add @import "htmx-ui/styles.css"; directly after @import "tailwindcss";. Call initComponents() on load and on htmx:after:process, as in step 4 above. Clashing variable names The library defines CSS variables such as --primary, --border and --radius on :root, and Tailwind colours with the same names. If your app already defines these, the definition loaded last wins. Rename yours, or set them to the values you want (see Theming).

sections.title: Already using the dark: variant?
sections.text: The library switches Tailwind's dark: variant from the OS media query to a .dark class on <html>. If your app relies on the media-query behaviour, read Dark mode before upgrading.

sections.title: What the package exports
sections.text: JavaScript ships as ES modules with TypeScript types. htmx.org and tailwindcss are peer dependencies, so your app controls their versions. Import Contents htmx-ui initComponents(root): wires up every component's behaviour under root. htmx-ui/styles.css Design tokens, the dark variant, .prose (Tailwind Typography, installed with the package), syntax-highlighting colours and every component's styles. htmx-ui/theme initTheme() and getTheme() for the light/dark switcher. htmx-ui/icons/.svg The SVG icons, for your own templates or tags. htmx-ui/components//.html Nunjucks macros (icon, code, alert, spinner). The engine resolves them by name: {% from "components/icon/icon.html" import icon %}.

pages.title: Engine
pages.description: htmx-ui-engine builds a site from Nunjucks pages: file-based routing, Tailwind, a dev server with hot reload and mock htmx endpoints, and static builds, on Bun or Node.

sections.text: htmx-ui-engine is the build tool behind npm create htmx-ui and this website. It turns a folder of HTML pages into a static site: each page is rendered with Nunjucks, then bundled (scripts and styles hashed and minified, Tailwind compiled from every class the page uses). The same engine runs on two runtimes: Runtime Dev server Build Tailwind Bun Bun.serve with HMR Bun.build bun-plugin-tailwind Node Vite with HMR Vite @tailwindcss/vite Both render pages with the same code, so a site builds the same way on either.

sections.title: Commands
sections.text: package.json { "scripts": { "dev": "htmx-ui dev", "build": "htmx-ui build", "preview": "htmx-ui preview" } } Command / option Description htmx-ui dev Dev server at http://localhost:3000 with hot reload: scripts and styles update in place; pages reload when a layout, partial, macro or data file changes. htmx-ui build Builds every page into dist/ (same paths as pages/), with scripts, styles and images in dist/assets/, content-hashed and shared by every page that uses them. Copies public/ next to it. htmx-ui preview Serves dist/ with the same clean URLs (/about for about.html). --port <n> Port for dev and preview. $PORT works too. --root <dir> Project root, if not the current directory. --bun, --node Pick the runtime (also HTMX_UI_RUNTIME=bun|node). The runtime follows whatever started the command: bun run dev and bunx htmx-ui run on Bun; npm run, pnpm, yarn and npx run on Node. Install the Tailwind integration for the one you use: bun add -d htmx-ui-engine tailwindcss bun-plugin-tailwind npm install -D htmx-ui-engine tailwindcss vite @tailwindcss/vite

sections.title: Project layout
sections.text: my-site/ pages/index.html -> / pages/about.html -> /about pages/docs/index.html -> /docs pages/docs/setup.html -> /docs/setup layouts/ partials/ shared templates data/*.json read from templates with json() public/ served at / and copied to dist/ as-is app.ts styles.css client entry and stylesheet htmx-ui.config.ts optional Pages, layouts and partials are covered in Templates & data. With htmx-ui installed, its macros and icons resolve by name, after your own files: {% from "components/icon/icon.html" import icon %}. Link files in public/ with a root-absolute URL (href="/favicon.svg"); they keep their names. Link everything else with asset(), so the bundler can hash it.

sections.title: Configuration
sections.text: Every option is optional, and a project without htmx-ui.config.ts uses the defaults. htmx-ui.config.ts import { defineConfig } from "htmx-ui-engine"; export default defineConfig({ pages: "pages", templates: ["."], outDir: "dist", publicDir: "public", url: "https://example.com", port: 3000, }); Option Description pages Routes directory. Default "pages". templates Template roots, searched in order. Default ["."]; htmx-ui's src/ is added last (ui: false turns that off). outDir Build output. Default "dist". publicDir Copied as-is. Default "public"; false to disable. url Public site URL, the origin template global. $SITE_URL overrides it. port Dev and preview port. Default 3000; $PORT overrides it. globals, filters Extra Nunjucks globals and filters. transform(html, page) Post-process every rendered page, in dev and build. routes Dev-only request handlers (see below). fetch(req) Dev-only fallback for anything else; return null for a 404. build.minify, build.sourcemap, build.define Production bundling options. build.done(ctx) Runs after a build with { outDir, pages }, e.g. to write a sitemap. vite Node only: extra Vite config, merged over the engine's.

sections.title: Mock htmx endpoints
sections.text:
While you build the front end, routes answers hx-get and hx-post with HTML fragments, so no backend is needed. Handlers take a web Request and return a Response, with Bun.serve's route syntax, on either runtime: htmx-ui.config.ts import { defineConfig } from "htmx-ui-engine"; const html = (body: string) => new Response(body, { headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html" } }); export default defineConfig({ routes: { "/api/users/:id": (req) => html(`

User ${req.params.id}

`), "/api/search": async (req) => { const q = new URL(req.url).searchParams.get("q") ?? ""; return html(`
  • Results for ${q}
    • `); }, }, }); Dev server only The build is static, so these routes don't exist in production. Point the same URLs at your real backend there.

sections.title: Use the plugins directly
sections.text: Already have a build script or a Vite config? Use the engine's plugin and skip the CLI: import { htmxUi } from "htmx-ui-engine/bun"; import tailwind from "bun-plugin-tailwind"; await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./pages/index.html", "./pages/about.html"], root: "./pages", outdir: "./dist", plugins: [await htmxUi(), tailwind], // htmx-ui first, so Tailwind sees rendered markup }); import { htmxUi } from "htmx-ui-engine/vite"; import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite"; export default { plugins: [htmxUi(), tailwindcss()], }; The package root, htmx-ui-engine, exports the runtime-independent core for your own tooling: defineConfig, loadConfig, render, renderPage, findPages, routeFor and highlight.

pages.title: Theming
pages.description: Every colour and corner in HTMX UI comes from a CSS variable. Override the variables to restyle the whole library; scope them to restyle part of a page.

headings.text: Using tokens in your own markup

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Theming happens in two layers, both in htmx-ui/styles.css: Variables. Plain custom properties on :root hold the actual values, with a second set under :root.dark. Tailwind colours. A @theme inline block maps each variable to a Tailwind colour, so --primary becomes bg-primary, text-primary, border-primary/30 and so on. htmx-ui/styles.css (excerpt) :root { --radius: 0.5rem; --primary: var(--color-indigo-600); --primary-foreground: var(--color-white); /* … */ } :root.dark { --primary: var(--color-indigo-500); /* … */ } @theme inline { --color-primary: var(--primary); --color-primary-foreground: var(--primary-foreground); /* … */ } Because the mapping is inline, the generated utilities read the variable at runtime: .bg-primary compiles to background-color: var(--primary). Change the variable anywhere (globally, under .dark, or on one element) and everything using it updates. No rebuild needed.

sections.title: Tokens
sections.text: Components only use these tokens. Swatches show the current theme; toggle dark mode in the header to compare. Variable Utility Used for Light Dark --background bg-background Page background white zinc-950 --foreground text-foreground Default text zinc-950 zinc-50 --surface bg-surface Cards, alerts, raised panels white zinc-900 --muted bg-muted Subtle fills: code, table heads zinc-100 zinc-800 --muted-foreground text-muted-foreground Secondary text zinc-500 zinc-400 --accent bg-accent Hover and selected backgrounds zinc-100 zinc-800 --accent-foreground text-accent-foreground Text on accent zinc-900 zinc-50 --border border-border Borders and dividers (the default border colour) zinc-200 zinc-800 --ring outline-ring Focus rings indigo-500 indigo-400 --primary bg-primary Brand colour: primary buttons, links indigo-600 indigo-500 --primary-foreground text-primary-foreground Text on primary white white --secondary bg-secondary Secondary buttons and badges zinc-100 zinc-800 --secondary-foreground text-secondary-foreground Text on secondary zinc-900 zinc-50 --info text-info Info alerts and badges sky-600 sky-400 --success text-success Success alerts and badges emerald-600 emerald-400 --warning text-warning Warning alerts and badges amber-600 amber-400 --danger bg-danger Destructive buttons, error alerts red-600 red-500 --danger-foreground text-danger-foreground Text on danger white white --scrollbar-thumb (scrollbars) Scrollbar thumb; every scrollbar is thin with a transparent track foreground at 16% foreground at 16% --scrollbar-thumb-hover (scrollbars) Scrollbar thumb while hovering the scroll area foreground at 32% foreground at 32% --radius rounded-(--radius) Corner radius for buttons, inputs, alerts; cards add 4px 0.5rem 0.5rem Values are Tailwind palette colours, for example var(--color-indigo-600). Any CSS colour works: hex, rgb(), oklch().

sections.title: Overriding tokens
sections.text: Redefine variables after importing the library. Set both the light and dark values for anything that should differ between them. src/styles.css @import "tailwindcss"; @import "htmx-ui/styles.css"; :root { --primary: oklch(0.6 0.2 30); /* coral */ --primary-foreground: white; --radius: 0.75rem; } :root.dark { --primary: oklch(0.7 0.17 30); } Selector specificity The library declares its tokens on :root and :root.dark inside @layer base. Unlayered CSS beats layered CSS, so overrides written outside any layer (as above) always win, whatever the import order.

sections.title: Custom themes
sections.text: A theme is just a selector that redefines tokens. Scope one to an attribute and you can apply it to a whole page or a single section. These previews use the same markup, with a different data-theme on each wrapper: default Pro Same markup, different tokens. Upgrade Later rose Pro Same markup, different tokens. Upgrade Later emerald Pro Same markup, different tokens. Upgrade Later src/styles.css [data-theme="rose"] { --primary: var(--color-rose-600); --ring: var(--color-rose-500); --radius: 1rem; } .dark [data-theme="rose"] { --primary: var(--color-rose-500); } html <!-- Whole page <!-- Whole page --> <html data-theme="rose"> <!-- Or one section <!-- Or one section --> <section data-theme="rose">…</section>

sections.title: Scrollbars
sections.text: The library styles every scrollbar to match: thin, with a transparent track and a thumb tinted from --foreground, so it blends into any theme and follows dark mode. Browsers without scrollbar-color (Safari) get the same look through ::-webkit-scrollbar. src/styles.css :root { --scrollbar-thumb: color-mix(in oklab, var(--primary) 30%, transparent); } /* Native scrollbars for one element */ .native-scrollbars { scrollbar-color: auto; scrollbar-width: auto; }

sections.title: Adding your own tokens
sections.text: Follow the same two steps to add a colour that Tailwind utilities can use: src/styles.css :root { --brand-gradient-from: var(--color-fuchsia-500); } :root.dark { --brand-gradient-from: var(--color-fuchsia-400); } @theme inline { --color-brand-from: var(--brand-gradient-from); } Now from-brand-from, text-brand-from and the rest are available, and they follow dark mode.

sections.title: Customising components
sections.text: Component classes live in @layer components, which sits below utilities. You can restyle them two ways: One element: add utilities. <button class="btn btn-primary rounded-full px-8"> gets a pill shape because utilities win. Everywhere: extend the class in your own @layer components block. src/styles.css @layer components { .btn { @apply font-semibold tracking-tight; } .card { @apply shadow-md; } }

sections.title: Using tokens in your own markup
sections.text: Use the token utilities instead of raw palette colours, and your own UI themes and switches modes with the library: html <aside class="rounded-(--radius) border border-border bg-surface p-4 text-muted-foreground"> Follows the theme and dark mode automatically. </aside>

pages.title: Dark mode
pages.description: Light and dark are two sets of token values, switched by a .dark class on <html>. The theme switcher follows the OS until the user picks, and never flashes the wrong theme.

headings.text: Avoiding a flash of the wrong theme

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: A class, not a media query. Tailwind v4's dark: variant normally follows prefers-color-scheme, which a button can't change. The library redefines it to match a .dark class instead. Tokens swap. :root.dark redefines every colour variable, so components don't need dark: classes at all. Native widgets follow. color-scheme switches too, so scrollbars and form controls match. htmx-ui/styles.css (excerpt) @custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *)); @layer base { :root { color-scheme: light; --background: var(--color-white); /* … */ } :root.dark { color-scheme: dark; --background: var(--color-zinc-950); /* … */ } }

sections.title: Theme switcher
sections.text: Any element with data-theme-toggle becomes a toggle. Try this one; it's the same toggle as the one in the header. html When clicked, initTheme() from htmx-ui/theme: flips the .dark class on , saves the choice to localStorage under the key theme, sets aria-pressed="true" on every toggle while dark is active, and writes the current theme (light or dark) into any [data-theme-label] inside a toggle. src/app.ts import { initTheme } from "htmx-ui/theme"; document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => initTheme());

sections.title: Following the OS
sections.text: Until the user clicks a toggle, the theme follows prefers-color-scheme and updates live when the OS changes. After a click, the stored choice wins. To go back to following the OS, clear it: ts localStorage.removeItem("theme");

sections.title: Avoiding a flash of the wrong theme
sections.text: Module scripts run after the first paint, so on a dark-mode visit the page would briefly render light. Put this tiny inline script in <head>, before your stylesheet and app script, so the class is set before anything is drawn: <head> <script> (() => { const stored = localStorage.getItem("theme"); const dark = stored ? stored === "dark" : matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches; document.documentElement.classList.toggle("dark", dark); })(); </script> Keep it in sync This script repeats the logic in initTheme(). If you change the storage key or the class name, change both.

sections.title: Writing dark styles
sections.text:
Prefer tokens: bg-surface and text-muted-foreground already adapt. For one-off tweaks, use the dark: variant as usual: html
Amber in light, a soft glow in dark.

sections.title: Forcing a theme
sections.text: To keep part of the page dark (a code sample, a hero) whatever the global theme, add the dark class to that element. Everything inside picks up the dark variant. Note that :root.dark tokens only apply at the root, so set the tokens you need on the element too: css .force-dark { --background: var(--color-zinc-950); --foreground: var(--color-zinc-50); --border: var(--color-zinc-800); color-scheme: dark; } html <section class="dark force-dark bg-background text-foreground">…</section>

sections.title: Building your own switcher
sections.text: getTheme() returns the active theme. A light/dark/system menu, for example, only needs to set or remove the stored value and toggle the class: ts import { getTheme } from "htmx-ui/theme"; function setTheme(choice: "light" | "dark" | "system") { if (choice === "system") localStorage.removeItem("theme"); else localStorage.setItem("theme", choice); const dark = choice === "system" ? matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches : choice === "dark"; document.documentElement.classList.toggle("dark", dark); } console.log(getTheme()); // "light" | "dark"

pages.title: Templates & data
pages.description: Pages are Nunjucks templates rendered at build time. They can read JSON files, inline SVGs and list files, so most content needs no API server.

sections.text: Optional The components are plain HTML and CSS, and work with any server or template language. This page covers the Nunjucks templates of htmx-ui-engine, which this site is built with too. Macros are new The package's Nunjucks macros (htmx-ui/components/*.html) need the engine's template helpers (svg(), json(), | dedent, | highlight). Their parameters may still change in a minor release before 1.0; each change is listed in the changelog.

sections.title: Pages and layouts
sections.text: Every .html file in pages/ is a route (docs/theming.html is /docs/theming). The engine renders it with Nunjucks before the bundler (Bun's or Vite) sees it, so pages can extend layouts, include partials and call macros. Template names resolve from the project root, then from the htmx-ui package (its components/ and icons/): pages/pricing.html {% extends "layouts/site.html" %} {% from "components/alert/alert.html" import alert %} {% block title %}Pricing · HTMX UI{% endblock %} {% block content %} {% call alert("Launch offer", variant="success") %}20% off the first year.{% endcall %} {% endblock %}

sections.title: JSON data
sections.text:
json(path) reads a JSON file at build time. Keep repeated content (navigation, pricing tiers, team members, release notes) in one file and render it anywhere, with no API and no client-side fetching. {% set releases = json("data/changelog.json").releases %}
    {% for r in releases %}
  • v{{ r.version }}, {{ r.date }}
    • {% endfor %}
{ "releases": [ { "version": "0.1.0", "date": "2026-10-02", "summary": "First release…" } ] } That template, live, reading this site's real file: v0.1.0, 2026-10-02 This site's data files: File (under site/) Description data/site.json Site name, description and URL (used for sitemaps). data/docs-nav.json Docs navigation: sidebar, prev/next, components index, page order for agents. data/changelog.json Releases, newest first. data/versions.json Docs versions; the latest is rendered live, older ones are archived.

sections.title: JSON in the browser too
sections.text: The same files can be imported by client code. Bun and Vite bundle them as plain objects: ts import nav from "./data/docs-nav.json"; console.log(nav.sections.length);

sections.title: SVG and icons
sections.text: svg(path, attrs) inlines an SVG file and sets attributes on its root, and the icon macro builds on it. Inlined SVG inherits colour and costs no extra requests. jinja {{ svg("icons/sun.svg", { class: "size-5 text-primary", "aria-hidden": "true" }) }}

sections.title: Listing files
sections.text: glob(pattern) returns matching paths across the template roots, sorted. The icon gallery is generated this way, from the package's icons/: jinja {% for path in glob("icons/*.svg") %}…{% endfor %}

sections.title: Reference
sections.text: Function / filter Description json(path) Parsed JSON file. Paths are relative to a template root (the project, then htmx-ui); first match wins. svg(path, attrs) Inline SVG with attributes set on the root <svg>. glob(pattern) Sorted list of root-relative paths matching the pattern. asset(path) Root-relative path rewritten relative to the current page (for <script src>, <link href>). url The current page's route, e.g. /docs/templates. origin The public site URL: url in htmx-ui.config.ts, or $SITE_URL. | dedent Remove shared indentation. | highlight(lang) Syntax-highlight a string at build time. All of them work inside imported macros too, without with context.

pages.title: AI agents
pages.description: Every docs page is published as Markdown, with an llms.txt index and JSON sitemaps, so coding agents can read the docs as specs.

headings.text: Use the docs for one task

sections.title: Markdown pages
sections.text: Add .md to any docs URL to get the page as Markdown: /docs/components/button.md, /docs.md. Each file starts with frontmatter (title, description, URL, section). Live examples become their source code, and reference tables become Markdown tables. The Copy Markdown button at the top of every page copies it for pasting into a chat. /docs/components/badge.md --- title: "Badge" description: "A small label for status, counts or categories." url: "/docs/components/badge" section: "Components" --- # Badge A small label for status, counts or categories. ```html New ```

sections.title: Indexes
sections.text: Each opens in a new tab. URL Contents /llms.txt llms.txt index (llmstxt.org): every docs page as a Markdown link with its description, grouped by section. Start here. /llms-full.txt Every docs page's Markdown in one file, for loading the whole library into context. /sitemap.json Every page with URL, Markdown URL, title, description, section, heading outline and section text, plus the list of docs versions. The index for site search. /docs/sitemap.json The same for the latest docs only. sections.title: How it's generated
sections.text: Nothing is written by hand. At build time the site's engine config (site/htmx-ui.config.ts) renders every page, converts the article body to Markdown (site/lib/markdown.ts), and writes the indexes (site/lib/site.ts). The dev server generates the same files on request. Page order follows the docs navigation in site/data/docs-nav.json. Absolute URLs (and the URLs in the prompts above) use the SITE_URL environment variable, falling back to url in site/data/site.json. Every docs heading gets an id and a # link, so sections can be linked directly. Add data-md-skip to an element to leave it out of the Markdown and the search text (purely visual blocks). Terminal SITE_URL=https://htmx-ui.example bun run build Write for both readers Agents read exactly what people read, so a clear page works for both. pages.description: Style long-form content without a class on every element: wrap it in .prose from @tailwindcss/typography, tuned to htmx-ui's tokens. Small helper classes cover single elements in UI chrome.

sections.title: Prose
sections.text:
Wrap plain HTML (an article, Markdown output, CMS content, a server-rendered fragment) in .prose. Every heading, paragraph, list, link, quote, table and code element inside is styled. No per-element classes. html

Shipping hypermedia

Your server already renders HTML. htmx swaps it in; htmx-ui makes it look good.

Return a fragment from any endpoint, point hx-target at it, and you're done. See installation.

  • Plain HTML in, styled content out
  • Works with Markdown renderers and CMS output

Hypermedia is the engine of application state.

Press Ctrl + K to search.

.prose comes from @tailwindcss/typography, which htmx-ui/styles.css loads for you. Everything in its docs works: sizes (prose-sm, prose-lg), element modifiers (prose-a:text-primary, prose-headings:tracking-tight), and max-w-none to drop the default line-length limit.

sections.title: What htmx-ui changes
sections.text: Colours come from the tokens: body and headings use --foreground, links --primary, rules and table borders --border, code blocks --code-background. Prose therefore follows custom themes and dark mode on its own. Don't add dark:prose-invert. Inline code is a pill on a muted background instead of being wrapped in backticks. Links get a soft underline that firms up on hover. Headings get scroll-margin-top so #anchor links clear a sticky header. Components placed inside prose with not-prose (alerts, code blocks, tables) get the same vertical spacing as paragraphs.

sections.title: Components inside prose
sections.text:
Prose styles every element inside it, which would also restyle a component's markup. Add not-prose to a component to keep its own styles. htmx-ui's Nunjucks macros (code, alert) already do. The flip side: .prose placed inside a not-prose element gets no styles at all, so don't nest them that way. html

pages.title: Toggle
pages.description: A two-state button that is either on or off. Any button variant can be a toggle.

sections.text: html <button class="btn btn-toggle btn-icon" data-toggle aria-pressed="false" aria-label="Bold"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" class="size-4" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M6 12h9a4 4 0 0 1 0 8H7a1 1 0 0 1-1-1V5a1 1 0 0 1 1-1h7a4 4 0 0 1 0 8"/></svg></button>

sections.title: Usage
sections.text: Add data-toggle and aria-pressed="false" (or "true" to start on) to any .btn. Each click flips aria-pressed, which screen readers announce as "pressed" or "not pressed". Styles key off the same attribute. The button fires a bubbling toggle:change event with detail.pressed. Keep the label the same in both states. "Bold" pressed reads correctly; switching the text to "Not bold" doesn't.

sections.title: Any button
sections.text: .btn-toggle is the dedicated look: muted when off, filled when on. Every other variant works too: ghost and outline fill when on, secondary turns the brand colour, and primary and danger are outlined when off and solid when on. sections.title: Components
sections.text: Accordion: built on <details>: one or several open, disabled items, bordered and separated styles, lazy-loaded content with htmx. Alert: neutral, info, success, warning and danger, with an optional dismiss button. Badge: solid, outline and soft status variants, plus a status dot. Button: primary, secondary, outline, ghost, danger and link variants; extra small to large sizes; icon, rounded, disabled and loading states. Button group: joins buttons, inputs, dropdowns and popovers: vertical, sized, separated, nested toolbars and split buttons. Card: header, title, description, action, content and footer parts; edge-to-edge images, horizontal layout, scrolling content, compact size and clickable cards. Code block: build-time syntax highlighting, copy button, file tabs and npm/pnpm/yarn/bun command tabs. Dropdown: accessible menu with keyboard navigation; powers the docs version switcher. Field: labels, descriptions and error, warning and success messages; an automatic required asterisk; inline, responsive and grid form layouts; fieldsets and separators. Icon: SVG files inlined at build time, or linked as images. Input: text inputs, textareas, selects and file inputs, with sizes and disabled, error, warning and success states. Input group: icons, text, badges, buttons, dropdowns and spinners inside an input, at the inline start or end, above or below. Popover: a floating panel of rich content or a small form that opens from a button. Sidebar: sticky on desktop, off-canvas with a backdrop on mobile. Spinner: any icon or a pure-CSS ring, in four sizes; works in buttons, badges, button groups and input groups, and as an htmx request indicator. Table: bordered wrapper, muted header and hover rows. Tabs: accessible tab groups that can sync with each other and remember the reader's choice. Text: @tailwindcss/typography (.prose) mapped onto the design tokens, plus heading, lead, muted, link, inline code and kbd helpers. Toggle: any button becomes an on/off toggle with aria-pres
